name: Luxora Collective closer contract review
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

The person is building out a sales team under The Luxora Collective and shared a 14-day trial independent contractor agreement for closers, asking Claude to review it and respond to notes from their assistant, Aanchal. The closer agreement mirrors an existing setter contract but is tailored for the sales closing role, with commission structures tied to different payment plans and partner continuation fees. Key protective clauses include a clawback provision, non-solicitation terms, IP assignment, and arbitration seated in Nashville.

The person had several open items: a minimum performance standard for Section 3.4, payout cadence, and per-contractor fill-ins. Claude recommended setting Section 3.4 at 2 Qualified Closed Clients OR a 25%+ close rate on calls taken, switching payout cadence from weekly to bi-weekly, adding a clawback reserve clause on final commissions post-termination, and defining the partner continuation fee structure either within the agreement or via a separate compensation schedule. Claude also advised keeping the 12-month non-solicitation and full IP assignment language as-is.

The person then asked Claude to reframe the full analysis as a direct reply to Aanchal that praised her work and incorporated the bottom line recommendations, then requested a shorter version of that message. The person's communication preference here was concise, direct, and structured with clear headers — maintaining substance while cutting length. Eric is referenced as someone involved in commission reconciliation, and William appears to be the first closer the agreement will be sent to.

chat_messages.text:
Reviewed the contract and Aanchal's note. Here's my read.

**Overall: this is solid.** It's tighter than most closer agreements I've seen at this stage. The clawback, attribution, and post-termination commission language all protect you properly. Mirroring the setter structure was the right call.

A few things to address before sending:

**1. Section 3.4 (Minimum Performance Standard during Trial)**

For a 14-day trial at $9k AOV, I'd anchor this to 2 Qualified Closed Clients. Here's the reasoning:

A competent closer working warm inbound discovery calls should close 20-30% on qualified leads. If William or future closers are getting 8-12 booked calls in a 14-day window (realistic for your current funnel), 2 closes is the floor for "this person can actually close." One is luck. Three+ is a star.

Don't go higher than 2 unless you're confident in your call volume. Setting it at 3 when your funnel only delivers 6 calls in 14 days punishes the contractor for your pipeline gaps, not their performance. That's a fast way to lose good closers and damage your reputation in the closer community (which is small and talks).

If you want to keep it stricter, alternative language: "2 Qualified Closed Clients OR a close rate of 25%+ on calls taken, whichever applies." This protects you if call volume is low and protects them if it's lower than expected.

**2. Payout cadence**

Switch to bi-weekly, not weekly. Here's why:

Weekly payouts on closer commissions create three problems for you:

First, the 72-hour guarantee window. You've structured commissions to only become earned AFTER the 72-hour refund window expires. If a deal closes on a Wednesday and you're paying out the following Friday, you're racing the clock on refund reconciliation, especially when payments process Thursday/Friday. Bi-weekly gives you breathing room.

Second, cash flow asymmetry. On the 2-month and 3-month plans, you're collecting installments monthly but paying commissions weekly. That mismatch isn't dangerous, but it's administratively annoying. Bi-weekly smooths it.

Third, administrative load on Eric. Weekly closer payouts means weekly reconciliation of: payments cleared, refunds processed, clawback offsets applied, partner continuation fees attributed. Bi-weekly cuts that workload in half without meaningfully impacting the contractor.

Monthly would be too long. Closers in this industry expect faster than monthly, and slow pay is the #1 reason good closers leave. Bi-weekly is the sweet spot: every other Friday, covering the prior two-week period.

Suggested replacement language for 4.6: "Commissions earned during a given two-week period (Monday through the second following Sunday) will be aggregated and paid to Contractor on the Friday following the close of each two-week period, or on such other regular payout schedule as Company may designate in writing."

**3. Effective Date and contractor name**

Standard, fill per individual at signing. No issue.

**A few things Aanchal didn't flag that you should consider:**

**Section 4.5(b) - Direct Recovery on clawbacks.** This is enforceable but in practice, recovering clawback money from a contractor who's already walked away is almost impossible without litigation that costs more than the clawback. Consider adding language that lets you hold the FINAL commission payment (or a percentage of recent payments) in reserve for 30-60 days post-termination as a clawback buffer. Something like:

"Upon termination, Company may retain up to fifty percent (50%) of any final commission payments otherwise due to Contractor for a period of sixty (60) days following termination, to be applied against any clawbacks that arise during such period. Any remaining amount shall be released to Contractor at the end of such period."

This is standard in closer contracts and far more effective than trying to chase money after the fact.

**Section 3.4 has a typo concern.** The blank reads "_____ (____)" which is the standard "two (2)" format. Just make sure when you fill it in, both the word and the numeral match. Easy to mess up.

**Partner Continuation Fee (4.1, 4.2(d)).** You haven't defined what the partner continuation fee structure actually is, just that 10% applies. If closers are pitching the partner continuation as part of their initial close (which they should be), they need to know the numbers. Either define them in the agreement or in a separate compensation schedule the contractor signs alongside. Otherwise, you'll get questions like "what am I actually selling them into after 90 days?"

**One thing to actively keep as-is:**

The 12-month non-solicit and the full IP assignment. Aanchal called these out as protections, and she's right. Don't soften them. In Tennessee these will hold up, and they protect you from the scenario where a closer takes your scripts, your prospect list, and your methodology to a competitor or starts their own thing targeting med spas. This is non-negotiable.

**Bottom line:** Fill 3.4 with 2, change payout to bi-weekly, add the clawback reserve clause, and define partner continuation fee structure (or reference a separate schedule). Then it's ready.

Want me to draft the redlines as clean replacement language you can drop into the doc?

input.summary_title: Reply to Aanchal on Closer Agreement
input.body:
This is excellent work. You anticipated the right questions, mirrored the setter structure cleanly, and flagged the exact spots where my input was needed instead of guessing. Exactly how I want these drafts to come to me.

Here's where I land on your open items, plus a few things to add before we send it out.

**1. Section 3.4, Minimum Performance Standard**

Set it at 2 Qualified Closed Clients OR a close rate of 25%+ on calls taken, whichever applies.

A competent closer on warm inbound should close 20 to 30% on qualified leads. Two is the floor for "this person can actually close." One is luck, three+ is a star. The OR clause protects us both ways: it protects us if a closer underperforms despite good call volume, and it protects them if our pipeline doesn't deliver enough calls in the 14-day window. That second piece matters because the closer community is small and talks, and we don't want a reputation for punishing contractors for our funnel gaps.

**2. Payout cadence: switch to bi-weekly**

Weekly is too tight on closer commissions for three reasons.

First, the 72-hour guarantee window. Commissions only become earned after that window expires. If a deal closes Wednesday and we're paying out the following Friday, we're racing the clock on refund reconciliation. Bi-weekly gives us breathing room.

Second, cash flow timing. On the 2-month and 3-month plans we're collecting monthly but paying weekly. That mismatch isn't dangerous but it's administratively messy.

Third, it cuts Eric's reconciliation workload in half (payments cleared, refunds processed, clawback offsets, partner continuation attribution) without slowing the contractor down in any meaningful way.

Monthly would be too slow, closers expect faster than that and slow pay is the top reason good closers leave. Bi-weekly is the right balance.

Replace 4.6 with: "Commissions earned during a given two-week period (Monday through the second following Sunday) will be aggregated and paid to Contractor on the Friday following the close of each two-week period, or on such other regular payout schedule as Company may designate in writing."

**3. Effective Date and contractor name**

Standard, fill per individual at signing. No changes needed.

**Three things to add before sending:**

**Clawback reserve clause in Section 4.5.** The direct recovery language is enforceable but in practice, recovering money from a contractor who's already walked away requires litigation that costs more than the clawback. Add a reserve buffer:

"Upon termination, Company may retain up to fifty percent (50%) of any final commission payments otherwise due to Contractor for a period of sixty (60) days following termination, to be applied against any clawbacks that arise during such period. Any remaining amount shall be released to Contractor at the end of such period."

This is standard in closer contracts and far more effective than chasing money after the fact.

**Define the Partner Continuation Fee structure.** We've said 10% applies but haven't defined what closers are actually selling into after 90 days. Either define the fee structure inside Section 4.1 or reference a separate compensation schedule the contractor signs alongside the main agreement. Otherwise closers will ask, and we want them confidently pitching this on the initial call.

**Typo check on 3.4.** When you fill in the minimum, double-check the word and numeral match. The "_____ (____)" format trips people up.

**Keep as-is:**

The 12-month non-solicit and full IP assignment are exactly right. Don't soften them. Tennessee will enforce both, and they protect us from the worst-case scenario of a closer leaving with our scripts, prospect list, and methodology.

**Bottom line:** Fill 3.4 with the 2 closes OR 25%+ close rate language, switch payout to bi-weekly, add the clawback reserve clause, and define the partner continuation fee structure (or reference a separate schedule). Then we're ready to send.

Send me the updated draft when you've made the changes and I'll do a final pass before it goes to William.

Thanks for the clean draft and the smart questions on this one.
